title: R-Row — ラ リ ル レ ロ

points.name: ラ
points.explanation: ラ makes the same 'ra' sound as hiragana ら — the Japanese flap consonant (between English 'r' and 'l') before the 'ah' vowel. Visually, ラ looks like a two-stroke character: a horizontal or slightly diagonal stroke at the top, and then a sweeping stroke descending to the lower right with a small foot. It resembles a stylized 'J' with a hat, or an angular hockey stick. Compare to hiragana ら, which has a more looping tail. ラ appears in ラジオ (radio), ランチ (lunch), and ラーメン (ramen) — one of Japan's greatest contributions to world cuisine.
rules: Same tongue-flap 'r' as ら — tap the alveolar ridge lightly, between English 'r' and 'l'.
ラ has two strokes: a horizontal hat + a sweeping descending stroke.
ラーメン (ramen) is perhaps the single most internationally famous Japanese food word.
points.flashcardAnswer: ra — same flap-R sound as ら; two strokes (hat + sweeping line)

points.name: リ
points.shortDescription: Same sound as り — 'ri' (tongue-flap R + ee)
points.explanation: リ makes the same 'ri' sound as hiragana り — the Japanese flap before the bright 'ee' vowel. Visually, リ is strikingly simple: just two vertical parallel strokes, like two parallel pillars or the Roman numeral 'II'. Compare to hiragana り, which also has two strokes but with the right stroke curving at the bottom into a small hook. The katakana リ's two straight strokes make it one of the cleaner, more geometric characters. リ appears in リモコン (remote control), リスト (list), and リラックス (relax).
rules: リ = two parallel vertical strokes. Very clean and geometric.
リモコン (remote control) is a common household term — everyone in Japan uses their リモコン daily!

examples.english: ice cream (リ in クリーム)

points.flashcardAnswer: ri — same flap-R+ee as り; looks like two parallel vertical strokes

points.name: ル
points.explanation: ル makes the same 'ru' sound as hiragana る — the Japanese tongue flap before the unrounded 'u' vowel. Visually, ル has a distinctive shape: two strokes — a vertical line, and then a stroke going right that angles down and curves to the lower right, ending in a small foot. It looks a bit like a 'J' hanging from a vertical pole, or the number '1' with a bottom-right curl. Compare to hiragana る, which is a complete loop. ル appears in ルール (rule), ルーム (room), and ルーツ (roots). ルール is an incredibly common word — Japanese people invoke rules constantly in everyday situations.
rules: Same flap-R + Japanese 'u' as る — flat, unrounded lips.
ル has two strokes: a vertical + a rightward stroke with a curling foot.
ルール (rule) is extremely common — you'll encounter it in sports, workplace, and social contexts.
points.flashcardAnswer: ru — same flap-R+u as る; looks like a 'J' hanging from a vertical stroke

points.name: レ
points.explanation: レ makes the same 're' sound as hiragana れ — the flap consonant before the 'eh' vowel. Visually, レ is perhaps the simplest R-row katakana: just two strokes — a short horizontal at the top that dips slightly, and then a long diagonal sweeping to the lower right. It resembles a checkmark or a swooping stroke. Compare to hiragana れ, which has a more complex branching tail. レ appears in レストラン (restaurant), レモン (lemon), and レンジ (range — used for microwave in Japan). レストランはどこですか? is essential dining vocabulary.
rules: レ = two strokes forming a swooping shape, like a checkmark or a 'J' without the top hook.
レストラン (restaurant) is a word you'll need from your very first meal out in Japan.
points.flashcardAnswer: re — same flap-R+e as れ; looks like a checkmark or swooping stroke

points.name: ロ
points.explanation: ロ makes the same 'ro' sound as hiragana ろ — the flap consonant before the 'oh' vowel. Visually, ロ is one of the most distinctive and memorable katakana characters: it's a simple rectangle or square, four strokes forming a box. Nothing more, nothing less. Compare to hiragana ろ, which looks like a backwards 'J'. The square shape of ロ is completely unique among katakana. ロ appears in ロボット (robot), ロック (rock — music or lock), and ロケット (rocket). Japan has one of the world's strongest robotics cultures, so ロボット comes up often in real contexts.
rules: ロ = a complete rectangle / square. The only katakana that is just a box — very easy to identify.
Memory: ロ looks like a little robot screen or window — fitting for ロボット (robot)!
points.flashcardAnswer: ro — same flap-R+o as ろ; looks like a square/rectangle — unique!

chapterPractice.prompt: What sound does this katakana make?
chapterPractice.explanation: ロ makes the 'ro' sound — same as hiragana ろ. It's the only katakana that looks like a complete rectangle or square, making it one of the easiest katakana to identify at a glance.

chapterPractice.prompt: Which hiragana makes the same sound as the katakana ル?
chapterPractice.explanation: ル and る are both read 'ru'. The R-row runs ラ/ら, リ/り, ル/る, レ/れ, ロ/ろ — the same five sounds in both scripts.

chapterPractice.prompt: What does this katakana word mean?
chapterPractice.explanation: ラーメン (raamen) means 'ramen' — the beloved Japanese noodle soup. ラ (ra) + ー (long vowel) + メ (me) + ン (n). One of Japan's most internationally recognized food exports.

chapterPractice.prompt: What does this katakana word mean?
chapterPractice.explanation: レストラン (resutoran) means 'restaurant'. レ (re) + ス (su) + ト (to) + ラ (ra) + ン (n). From French 'restaurant'. Essential vocabulary for dining out in Japan.
